The United Arab Emirates currently operates one crude export pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz and announced earlier this year that it was building a second. A third pipeline is reportedly being planned to further expand crude capacity and reroute energy flows around Hormuz, reducing exposure to Iranian disruption and weakening Tehran's leverage over the critical maritime chokepoint. Bloomberg reported Wednesday morning that Abu Dhabi’s state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co., is weighing plans for a third pipeline from the UAE’s western coast to Fujairah on its eastern coast that could supply Asian customers and bypass Hormuz. "Adnoc has been telling some customers in Asia about the pipeline, other people familiar with the matter said. The plans haven’t been finalized and could still change, including the route, a number of the people said," the outlet reported. The new pipeline would build on the UAE's existing pipeline, which has operated since 2012 and stretches 252 miles from Habshan in Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. That pipeline has a capacity of 1.5 million barrels a day, expandable to 1.8 million. Earlier this year, the UAE announced the West-East Pipeline, expected to begin operations in 2027 and double export capacity through Fujairah. Notably, Fujairah sits outside the Hormuz chokepoint, allowing tankers to load crude without entering the Persian Gulf. An ADNOC spokesperson responded to the outlet's request for comment: “We have advised Bloomberg that this report is not accurate and purely speculative.” Beyond the UAE, the biggest story of the year has been other US-allied Gulf countries expanding pipeline routes around Hormuz, including Saudi Arabia , while Kuwait is proposing new pipelines. body: Copper prices plunged to a three-month low this week as fears over the AI boom spread from technology stocks into commodities. On Tuesday, copper fell 3.2% to $13,883 per ton on the London Metal Exchange. Prices recovered on Wednesday, climbing back above $14,100 following the US midterm elections . The metal has now retreated from its September record of $14,875, raising questions about whether its historic rally is losing momentum. First, the recent AI stock market rout has shaken confidence in the spending boom behind new data centers. Copper is essential for electrical infrastructure, making it a popular investment tied to AI expansion. Marex analyst Ed Meir said copper appeared to be “catching up” with the recent semiconductor selloff. Second, Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress has reduced expectations of US tariffs on refined copper. Those tariff fears previously encouraged traders to stockpile copper in America, squeezing supplies elsewhere and pushing prices higher. Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen warned that reduced tariff expectations could hurt copper prices. The surprising development is that physical copper demand remains relatively strong. China’s Yangshan copper premium, a measure of demand for imported metal, remains near $200 per ton, its highest in more than a decade. Meanwhile, Chinese warehouse inventories have fallen more than 75% in six months. Investors are selling copper over economic uncertainty while physical buyers continue competing for limited supplies. On the daily copper chart , prices remain in a descending channel after breaking their upward trendline. The $6.31-per-pound area is critical support, near July’s low. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth. Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest. Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday. The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less. Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand. Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree. The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months. At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports. The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter. Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: The data offer something for both sides of the BoJ debate: historically sharp cost pressures support further tightening, while slowing hiring and weaker confidence give the cautious camp ammunition. On balance, the release is unlikely to shift December pricing materially, leaving the yen more sensitive to the BoJ minutes and oil-driven inflation signals. Firms citing inflation as a drag on confidence underlines how energy costs from the Middle East are feeding into Japanese business sentiment. Weak export orders point to limited support from overseas demand. Japan’s service providers are still growing and still paying up, but they’re hiring less and feeling gloomier about it. Japan’s services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in October, but a slowdown in manufacturing pulled overall private sector growth to a five-month low, while still-sharp cost pressures kept inflation in focus for the Bank of Japan, according to S&P Global’s latest survey. The S&P Global Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, marking a fifth straight month of expansion. Firms said stronger inflows of new work and efforts to broaden their customer base lifted activity, though growth remained modest and below the average so far this year. New orders also picked up slightly, driven by firmer domestic demand. Export business fell again, although the decline was the smallest in six months. Hiring was the weak spot. Services employment rose only marginally, the slowest pace in the current 14-month run of job creation, as some firms reported staff leaving through resignations and retirements. With capacity stretched, backlogs of work increased again. Price pressures slowed but stayed elevated. Input cost inflation fell to an eight-month low and output charges also rose more slowly, yet both remained well above their long-run averages. Business confidence about the year ahead dropped to its weakest since March, with firms citing inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages. The broader picture was softer. The composite PMI, which combines services and manufacturing, slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its lowest since May, though it still pointed to a 19th consecutive month of growth. Faster services growth was offset by a slower rise in factory output. Across the private sector, job creation slowed to a one-year low and confidence fell to a three-month low. Input costs rose at a historically sharp rate, while growth in prices charged eased to a four-month low. S&P Global said input costs and selling prices, while rising more slowly, were still increasing at a pace that suggests official consumer inflation could stay elevated in the coming months. It added that whether growth loses further momentum and whether cost pressures ease will be key considerations for the BoJ as it weighs further tightening, warning that persistent inflation weighed on confidence and could also constrain demand and hiring. The data arrive on the same day as minutes from the BoJ’s September meeting, which showed policymakers agreed on the need for further rate increases, keeping attention on whether the central bank moves again in December. Korea bore the brunt. The exchange also said trading will open an hour late on November 19 to keep roads clear for the national university entrance exam. In Tokyo, the market divided along the same line. The broad Topix rose about 1.4%, led by real estate, retail and pharmaceuticals, while the tech-heavy Nikkei fell about 1.5% as chip equipment makers Advantest and Tokyo Electron slumped. Most Nikkei members rose, but losses in a handful of heavily weighted tech stocks dragged the index lower. Sony and Nintendo report after the close. SoftBank Group fell about 5.8% to around ¥4,020. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… A majority of European Union citizens are in favor of an accelerated transition away from oil and gas and into alternative energy sources and transport electrification, a survey conducted by the European Investment Bank has shown, as reported by Reuters, which got an exclusive look at the survey. According to the survey, which involved 23,000 respondents, 87% wanted governments to make the transition a priority, with 52% saying solar should be at the top of the list of alternative, low-carbon energy sources. Nuclear, on the other hand, had only 19% saying it should be prioritized. The percentage in favor of wind as a top alternative energy source stood at 37%. “In a rapidly shifting geopolitical landscape, this is both the right thing to do for the planet and the smart thing to do for our economies, in order to bring down energy costs for businesses and households,” the president of EIB Group, Nadia Calvino, told Reuters. Calvino’s second point is interesting because over the past decade since the Paris Agreement was signed, the EU member states that spent the most on wind, solar, and electric vehicle support saw their electricity prices rise the most as well, while transition laggards have managed to keep bills relatively affordable. The war between the U.S., Israel, and Iran has highlighted the drawbacks of energy import dependence and strengthened the argument for locally sourced energy, especially from wind and solar installations, but also oil and gas where it is present. Proponents argue that both of these, especially solar, are already cheaper than gas generation. Critics note the cost estimates for wind and solar are based on levelized cost of energy metrics that exclude a lot of actual costs, such as the cost of electricity that needs to come from a baseload generator when there is no sun or, indeed, wind. summary: One policymaker voted to raise the bank's key interest rate to 4.25%.
body: The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%. The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago. The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%. "The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level." Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027. "It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said. Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December. Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside." "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said. Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war. The MPC's most hawkish member, Catherine L Mann, said she had voted for greater tightening than her peers because research pointed to "non-linear inflation risks." "My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a 'down payment' to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold 'good policy'," she said in comments published in the MPC's policy statement. "The economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects," Mann added. "A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off... From a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy'." Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, had been rising before the policy announcement and continued to edge higher after the Bank of England's update. The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was last seen 2 basis points higher at 5.1546%, while the 2-year gilt yield rose by 4 basis points to trade at 4.782%. The British pound , which hit a post-Brexit high on Wednesday, was flat against both the U.S. dollar and the euro on Thursday afternoon. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note on Thursday that the November hike was "hugely symbolic." "The path ahead remains uncertain with much depending not only on how oil trades but also on natural gas prices which have risen sharply over the past few months. body: Bitcoin CME futures swept to $75,795 and rebounded on unusually heavy trading. The four-hour recovery is encouraging, but holding $79,040 and clearing $81,460 would tell us much more about whether buyers have genuinely regained control. Bitcoin CME futures have changed character in the space of a few sessions. After aggressive selling and repeated attempts to extend the decline, the market briefly broke below $76,000, recovered, and then rallied to $81,460 on November 4. It is a promising short-term reversal attempt, but the difference between a rebound and a lasting change of trend still matters. The starting point is straightforward: sellers achieved a fresh low but could not sustain the breakdown. Buyers then produced a much more decisive upward move. That echoes the lesson in Greg Michalowski's earlier Bitcoin analysis of sellers failing to extend a support break . His article examines different Bitcoin price references, so the levels in this CME futures analysis should be evaluated on their own terms. October 29: Sellers set the tone. CME Bitcoin futures traded as high as $82,270 before reversing. One four-hour candle fell from an $81,525 open to a $79,045 close. Another ended at $77,025 on volume of 4,141 contracts. There was no need to guess who had the advantage then: the price was moving substantially lower. October 30: Trading activity remained intense, but downside progress became less convincing. A four-hour candle traded between $76,550 and $78,200 on 4,576 contracts, yet opened at $77,425 and closed at $77,420, a net loss of just $5. That does not prove buyers were accumulating Bitcoin. It does show a great deal of trading without a meaningful change between the open and close. November 3: The break below the lows failed. A later four-hour candle fell to $75,795, undercutting earlier lows around $76,260-$76,450, then closed back at $77,905. This could have been a liquidity sweep , when a price move through a well-watched low triggers orders but fails to establish a new lower trading range. We can see the failed break in the price data; we cannot independently verify the stop orders or intentions behind it. November 4: Buyers finally generated meaningful upward displacement. A four-hour candle opened at $78,535, climbed to $81,460 and closed at $80,655, with volume of 5,468 contracts. That was about 5.1 times the preceding 20-bar average of 1,066 contracts. The comparison is striking, although the average includes thinly traded periods around the weekend, so the multiple should not be treated as a calibrated signal. By the last completed four-hour bar in the supplied November 5 snapshot, futures had closed at $80,925. The following bar was still developing. These are dated CME continuous-futures observations, not a live Bitcoin spot quote . Volume measures how much trading took place. It does not, by itself, tell us which side is winning. Compare the two unusually active four-hour candles. On October 30, 4,576 contracts accompanied a candle body of minus $5 . On November 4, 5,468 contracts accompanied a candle body of plus $2,120 . There was plenty of activity on both occasions, but only the second produced a decisive net change in price. The first pattern is consistent with buyers meeting aggressive selling or with two-sided trading. The second is stronger evidence that buyers were able to push prices higher. Neither observation proves institutional accumulation, trapped short positions or a particular order-flow mechanism. US stocks soared on Wednesday after President Donald Trump's party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6% for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 3%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4%. Stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump's social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. "Earnings trump elections," according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have got a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy. Much remains impossible to predict and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and, in some instances, trade. A downbeat forecast could be that "Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck" who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies' levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. title: Expedia CEO says AI agents aren't changing booking habits — yet
summary: Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin told CNBC that AI agents present an exciting time for the travel industry but that they haven't yet impacted bookings.
body: Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin said Thursday the company hasn't yet seen artificial intelligence agents affecting the way customers book, but the early signs show potential for an industry shift. "It's a great way for people to do inspiration, to do trip planning," Gorin said in an interview with CNBC. "We haven't seen it change the way they're actually doing booking." The comments come as personal AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots enter the mainstream, promising to tackle everything from scheduling to shopping for everyday Americans. Opportunities in travel planning and booking could pose a competitive threat to traditional sites like Expedia. Gorin said Expedia is "working with all of the agents" to make sure it surfaces in AI results, to understand how the agents get information and to make sure that the company has the necessary integrations. She acknowledged it's possible that AI agents could develop their own travel programs and eventually claim market share, but she said complexities within the industry — customer service, for example — would be difficult to fully replace with artificial intelligence. "People were already shopping across a number of places, so the agent can do that in a much easier way," Gorin said. "But when it comes to actually booking — being confident that the content that you're getting is right, the amenities are right, the price is right, if something goes wrong, someone's going to actually either solve it for you, answer the phone, be there for you — I don't think those agents are going to do it for you, and that's why people trust Expedia and come to us." Shares of Expedia were down about 12% Thursday after the company delivered weaker-than-expected guidance for the fourth quarter on Wednesday. The company forecast revenue of between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion for the final three months of the year, making the midpoint lower than analyst estimates of $3.74 billion, according to FactSet. Gorin attributed the "moderation" in Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance to "geopolitical events in the Middle East and Europe," the midterm elections and the company moving its fall sale from the fourth quarter to the third quarter. But she noted the company reported a strong third quarter , as total gross bookings rose 11% and revenue climbed 12%.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes its Productivity and Costs report quarterly. A preliminary estimate comes out roughly five weeks after the quarter ends, followed by a revised estimate about a month later that incorporates updated GDP and labor data. The headline measure is labor productivity in the nonfarm business sector, defined as output per hour worked. It’s reported as an annualized quarterly rate and as a year-over-year change. Output is derived from GDP, excluding government, households, nonprofits and farms, while hours come from the BLS employment surveys. Productivity growth is the main long-run driver of living standards, because it determines how fast incomes can rise without generating inflation. Unit labor costs measure what businesses pay in compensation to produce one unit of output. They’re calculated as hourly compensation divided by productivity. When wages rise faster than productivity, unit labor costs climb, which can squeeze profit margins or push companies to raise prices. That makes the measure a closely watched input in the inflation outlook and in the Federal Reserve’s assessment of whether wage growth is consistent with its 2% target. The report also includes figures for manufacturing and for nonfinancial corporations, along with hourly compensation and real hourly compensation. The quarterly numbers are noisy and prone to large revisions, particularly as GDP and compensation data are updated. For that reason, economists tend to focus on multi-quarter and annual trends. The report rarely moves markets, but productivity has drawn renewed attention as investors and policymakers look for signs that artificial intelligence is lifting output per worker and allowing faster growth without added inflation. Her… U.S. refineries are producing a smaller share of gasoline from every barrel of crude oil they process and shifting production efforts toward diesel and jet fuel as soaring margins on those products reshape the economics of American refining. Gasoline yields averaged below 45% during the first eight months of 2026, falling below the previous five-year low in every month, according to data published Thursday by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). That's a significant departure for a refining industry that typically produces 45 to 50 barrels of gasoline for every 100 barrels of crude processed. And even though gasoline prices are elevated, diesel and jet fuel are considerably more profitable to produce as global fuel shortages drive refining margins higher. Distillate fuel oil yields, which include diesel and heating oil, exceeded their five-year average in every month through August. Jet fuel production has undergone an even more pronounced shift. In March, jet fuel's share of U.S. refinery output exceeded 12% for the first time on record. It remained at or above that level through August, the latest month for which EIA data is available. The changes reflect an increasingly strained global refining market. The Iran war has disrupted Middle Eastern refining operations, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have further restricted supplies of diesel and other petroleum products. Global refinery crude runs dropped by 4.8 million barrels per day in the second quarter, according to EIA data released earlier this week. Although throughput recovered by 1.8 million bpd in the third quarter, it remained approximately 5% below year-earlier levels. U.S. refineries, meanwhile, increased crude processing by 500,000 bpd in the second quarter and another 500,000 bpd in the third, helping compensate for lost production elsewhere. Diesel prices reached their highest nominal levels on record in September. For U.S. refiners, the opportunity extends beyond processing more crude. The shortage has changed which fuels deliver the greatest returns, encouraging refiners to maximize middle distillates even at the expense of gasoline yields. The result is a domestic refining system increasingly oriented toward supplying a global market short of diesel and jet fuel. body: Turkey targets total investments of $500 billion in energy infrastructure in its new energy plan to 2040, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Alparslan Bayraktar, said on Thursday, as the country looks to boost its energy independence and eventually become energy independent. In recent years, Turkey has been paying up to $70 billion to import energy, including coal, oil, and gas. The new energy plan looks to slash the import bill while strengthening the homegrown resources, including gas in the Black Sea and a fourfold jump in installed solar and wind power capacity. Turkey aims to meet its energy needs with homegrown resources and to implement a total investment of $500 billion in its energy infrastructure by 2040, minister Bayraktar said today. Turkey plans to meet all its petroleum and natural gas consumption through domestic resources, and boost its wind and solar installed capacity fourfold to 175 gigawatts (GW) by 2040. The country looks to raise the share of renewable energy of its installed electricity-generation capacity to 77%, and build 10 GW of nuclear power capacity, the minister said. Akkuyu , Turkey’s first nuclear power plant, is currently being built by Russia’s Rosatom. With a total capacity of 4,800 MW, the nuclear power plant is expected to meet around 10% of the Turkish power demand. In the new era of mobility, Turkey will also target 20 million electric vehicles (EVs) by 2040, while policies to increase energy efficiency are expected to bring $240 billion in savings, Bayraktar said. Last year, Turkey ranked fourth in Europe in EV sales, with 190,000 fully electric vehicles sold, or 17% of total new car sales, energy think tank Ember says . The share of solar and wind in Turkey is about 22%, but coal currently remains the single biggest power-generating source with 34%, according to data by Ember. Investments in the electricity projects alone would require more than $200 billion in investment, according to Reuters calculations. In a significant, albeit underreported development for global energy, and for the US-Iran standoff in the Persian Gulf, the Iranian parliament has this week announced it is exempting several key trading partners from its oil transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. The move was first unveiled Tuesday by Ahmad Hayat-Moghaddam, Vice Chairman of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, at a moment when Iranian export flows are struggling under the many months-long US naval blockade of the country's ports. "We have currently exempted India, China, Iraq and Qatar from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Ships from these countries pass freely," Hayat-Moghaddam stated in an interview to the Iranian Student’s News Agency (SNA). He described that this also aimed at shoring up "mutual interests" among countries that have long done business with one another. The Iranian official also sought to frame the change as arising out of joint humanitarian concerns : Tehran is facilitating the movement of Indian ships for the purpose of medicines, while Chinese ships are exempted from the restrictions to “secure” Beijing’s political support, Hayat-Moghaddam told SNA. His comments suggested further that the US Navy doesn't block these ships from passing, which could explain how Iran has continued to get oil and wares out to global markets despite the blockade. "The Americans do not interfere with them either," he claimed. Elaborating on the rationale behind the decision, the lawmaker noted that the Islamic Republic does not levy transit tolls on Qatari vessels and that each exemption was granted based on specific considerations and agreements. Hayat-Moghaddam remarked: “We are conducting business, and each of these exemptions has a distinct reason.” According to the MP, India’s exemption was designed to facilitate medicine imports into Iran, while China’s exemption aims to secure political backing from Beijing for the Islamic Republic. October saw a record number of attacks on commercial vessels by Iran, keeping geopolitical risk elevated across the region; however, what was a near-daily pace of the attacks seems to have slowed, for now. Even global media reporting has slowed in terms of an Iranian focus, having given way to the midterm elections and major Democratic gains in the US. President Trump has still held off on prior threats to resume a major bombing campaign after the midterm elections - but this is a possibility still on the table. title: AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit
summary: The investment comes as the gold miner aims to incrementally increase production by the end of the decade.
body: AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) plans to invest up to $900 million in expanding brownfield operations across its portfolio, targeting a production increase of 300,000 ounces to 450,000 ounces by 2030. The investments will focus on the Geita gold mine in Tanzania, Siguiri in Guinea and Cuiabá in Brazil, as well as the ongoing ramp-up at Obuasi in Ghana. The company expects the projects to generate real internal rates of return exceeding 35%, Reuters reported. “These are high-return, capital efficient projects at our operating mines that are expected to provide high-margin ounces and unlock further value from our portfolio,” AngloGold Ashanti CEO Alberto Calderon said in a statement. The plan is to use existing infrastructure and operational footprints to reduce risk and optimize capital intensity. Geita will receive the larger portion of the funding, up to $580 million to raise output to 600,000 ounces by 2030. Cuiabá’s expansion will cost between $200 million and $250 million, adding about 75,000 ounces to its output. Another $70 million will be put towards the Suguiri mine, looking to add another 100,000 ounces to its production. Shares in AngloGold Ashanti were up 0.35% to $88.22 apiece by mid-day Thursday in New York, valuing the company at $44.6 billion. AngloGold reported a 12% increase for its EBITDA for Q3 2026 to $1,568 million, from $1,400 million for Q3 2025. The company said on its Q3 earnings release that the growth is supported by the increase in the average gold price received per ounce to $4,239/oz, from $3,490/oz in the same period in 2025. AngloGold Ashanti said its full year gold production guidance of 2,800,000 ounces to 3,170,000 ounces is reaffirmed. Its gold production was about 3.65% more costly than the previous quarter, at $1,534 per ounce due gold royalties and higher fuel costs. The company also reported that a worker died due to a rockfall at the Sukari underground mine in August 2026. Operations were suspended while investigations took place, but have since resumed. title: Chibougamau offers copper growth for Central Asia: BMO
summary: Annual steady-state production at Chibougamau could hit about 20,000 tonnes of copper and 32,000 oz. of gold.
body: Central Asia Metals ’ (AIM, TSX: CAML) newly acquired Chibougamau project in Quebec could produce more copper annually than the company’s Kounrad mine, helping offset declining output at the Kazakhstan operation in the early 2030s, according to BMO Capital Markets. Annual steady-state production at Chibougamau could hit about 20,000 tonnes of copper and 32,000 oz. of gold, with first output set for late 2031 or early 2032, BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Alexander Pearce said Wednesday in a note. Pearce resumed coverage at outperform, while cutting his share-price target by 25% to 180 pence (C$3.38) from 240 pence. Chibougamau could more than replace the copper output Central Asia expects to lose as Kounrad declines. But that growth would require substantial investment: BMO assumes C$630 million ($450 million) in pre-production capital, including replacement of the existing mill, with permitting likely to determine when construction can begin. “While the project is early stage and many unknowns remain, its existing infrastructure and potential resource upside via its hub-and-spoke model are key positives,” Pearce wrote. Central Asia shares rose 2.1% to C$2.41 Thursday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$618 million ($441 million). They’ve ranged between C$2.26 and C$2.59 since the stock began trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange last week. BMO is assuming Chibougamau will require three years of construction for annual mill throughput of 900,000 tonnes. An updated preliminary economic assessment is expected in the second half of 2027. Central Asia inherited Chibougamau when it completed its acquisition of Cygnus Metals Oct. 27. Cygnus shareholders received 0.06 Central Asia shares for each share held. The Canadian project adds potential replacement production as Kounrad declines. An August reserve update forecast copper output at the mine could drop to 9,000 tonnes in 2031 and 6,000 tonnes in 2032, with production continuing through 2034. Central Asia’s 2026 target remains 12,000–13,000 tonnes. Kounrad recovers copper from historical waste dumps in Kazakhstan. London-based Central Asia also operates the Sasa zinc-lead mine in North Macedonia. Located about 480 km north of Montreal, Chibougamau covers more than 282 sq. km. Its Copper Rand processing plant last operated in 2008 and has historical capacity of 900,000 tonnes a year. Central Asia says the plant requires refurbishment, but BMO assumes it will be replaced. The project also has tailings storage, a hydroelectric power connection and road and rail infrastructure. Five deposits — Corner Bay, Devlin, Cedar Bay, Joe Mann and Golden Eye — lie within about 50 km of the plant and could supply a central mill. A September 2025 estimate for Chibougamau estimated the property holds measured and indicated resources of 6.4 million tonnes grading 2.3% copper, 0.8 gram gold per tonne and 7.6 grams silver per tonne for contained metal of 149,000 tonnes copper, 167,000 oz. gold and about 1.6 million oz. silver. Inferred resources total 8.5 million tonnes grading 2.1% copper, 1.7 grams gold per tonne and 7.9 grams silver per tonne, containing 182,000 tonnes copper, 454,000 oz. gold and about 2.2 million oz. silver. No mineral reserves have been established at Chibougamau. Further studies must determine the mine plan, capital requirements and operating costs before BMO’s conceptual production case can be tested. title: Rio Tinto injects $144 million into Resolution Copper after land battle win
summary: Fresh funding will advance engineering and underground development at the Arizona project as legal and cultural tensions persist.
body: Rio Tinto (ASX, LON: RIO) has approved a $144 million investment to advance its Resolution Copper project in Arizona, months after securing control of land needed for what could become one of the largest copper mines in the US. The funding will support feasibility studies and engineering work for mining equipment and water treatment facilities. Rio Tinto will contribute $79 million, reflecting its 55% stake in the joint venture, while BHP (ASX: BHP) will cover the remaining 45% . The companies expect the next phase to create about 50 additional jobs. “Resolution Copper has the potential to supply up to 25% of America’s copper demand for decades, strengthen domestic supply chains and deliver significant economic benefits for Arizona,” Rio Tinto chief executive, copper, Katie Jackson said in a statement. The investment underscores Rio Tinto’s growing focus on copper as demand rises for the metal used in power grids, electrification and artificial intelligence infrastructure. It also marks another step toward developing a major domestic supply source as the US seeks to strengthen its critical minerals supply chains. The decision follows a lengthy legal battle over the transfer of federal land needed for the mine. The dispute pitted the religious rights of the San Carlos Apache people against efforts to develop one of the country’s largest undeveloped copper deposits. Native American groups have opposed the project because of its potential impact on the Oak Flat, a site considered sacred by Apache communities. Although Rio Tinto secured control of the acreage, the controversy has highlighted the challenges of balancing mineral development with Indigenous cultural and religious protections. Located near Superior, Arizona, the copper deposit lies between 5,000 and 7,000 feet (1,524 and 2,134 metres) underground. Rio Tinto has targeted the mid-2030s for the mine’s opening, although the development remains subject to further studies and approvals. The project is estimated to contain more than 40 billion lb. (18.1 million tonnes) of copper, with the potential to support production for decades. The latest commitment builds on about $110 million in contracts awarded by Resolution Copper in August for exploration and underground development at the site. Rio Tinto, the world’s largest iron ore producer, has increasingly sought to expand its copper business as demand for the metal accelerates. Strong copper contributions helped drive its half-year earnings higher in July, reinforcing the commodity’s importance to the company’s long-term growth strategy. The joint venture estimates that Resolution Copper could generate thousands of jobs and contribute about $1 billion annually to Arizona’s economy once operational. The mine’s scale, technical complexity and history of legal opposition remain significant hurdles. Developing a deposit at such depths will require substantial infrastructure and investment before commercial production can begin. title: Lundin cuts copper outlook again as wild Chile weather bites
summary: Its Caserones mine faces a prolonged recovery after winter weather disrupted mining, even as record metal prices boost cash flow.
body: Lundin Mining (TSX: LUN) has lowered its 2026 copper production forecast for the second time in two months as lingering damage from severe winter storms in Chile continues to hamper operations at its Caserones mine. The Canadian miner cut Caserones’ full-year guidance to 105,000–115,000 tonnes from 120,000–130,000 tonnes, bringing its company-wide forecast to 285,000–310,000 tonnes. The latest revision follows an August reduction from an initial target of 130,000–140,000 tonnes. “Importantly, these are deferred tonnes rather than lost production, and we expect to see a recovery in operational performance through 2027,” the company said in its third-quarter results. The repeated cuts highlight the operational challenges facing Lundin at one of its key Chilean assets, even as record copper prices strengthen its balance sheet and help fund an expanding pipeline of growth projects. Caserones’ recovery will be important to restoring production momentum next year. Severe winter storms suspended operations at Caserones for about 30 days during the third quarter, while subsequent snowmelt has continued to restrict haulage rates and ore deliveries to the mill into the fourth quarter. Lundin produced 62,610 tonnes of copper in the three months ended Sept. 30, matching BMO Capital Markets’ estimate of 62,600 tonnes but falling short of the 68,000-tonne analyst consensus, BMO analyst Matthew Murphy said in a note on Thursday. Gold production reached 36,763 oz., exceeding BMO’s 34,900-oz. forecast and roughly matching consensus expectations of 37,300 ounces. Despite the weaker output, Lundin maintained Caserones’ cash cost guidance at $2.15–$2.35 per lb., following an increase in August, and reduced sustaining capital expenditure guidance by $20 million to $215 million. Consolidated cash cost guidance remains at $1.95–$2.15 per lb. Other operations performed more strongly. Copper production at the Candelaria complex in Chile rose 13% from the second quarter, while Brazil’s Chapada mine recorded its highest quarterly copper and gold output of the year. Record realized copper prices helped Lundin Mining generate more than $1.1 billion in quarterly revenue, marking its fourth consecutive quarter above $1 billion. Free cash flow from operations reached $418 million, leaving the company with a net cash position of $237 million at quarter-end. “Supported by record realized copper prices in the year to date, our adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) of $1.9-billion and free cash flow from operations of $1.2-billion have both already surpassed their full-year 2025 totals, positioning the company for what we expect to be another record beating financial year,” president and CEO Jack Lundin said. At Caserones, the company is pursuing leach optimization initiatives aimed at raising copper cathode production to the plant’s existing annual capacity of 35,000 tonnes. At Chapada, construction of an additional ball mill is about 15% complete, with commissioning targeted for late 2027. title: Codelco’s inflated copper output scandal hits 42,100 tonnes
summary: Chile's state miner faces scrutiny over mounting debt, falling returns and costly investments as its board charts a recovery.
body: Chile’s state-owned copper giant Codelco has identified 42,100 tonnes of artificially inflated production in its reporting, exposing weaknesses in internal controls as the miner struggles with declining output, rising costs and mounting debt. Board chairman Bernardo Fontaine disclosed the figure Thursday at an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting, adding that a separate irregularity had affected 17,000 tonnes of copper inventory valued at between $120 million and $140 million. “Recent incidents related to production figures have affected confidence in Codelco and its reputation. There’s no point in denying it,” Fontaine said . The revelations deepen concerns about Codelco’s turnaround after production fell to two-decade lows in 2022 and 2023. As one of the world’s largest copper producers, the company plays a critical role in global supply as demand grows from electrification, power grids, electric vehicles and AI data centres. Codelco has ordered audits and dismissed nine employees across three mines and its corporate offices as it investigates whether production figures were overstated. “This is a serious issue because it reveals weaknesses in control, traceability and operational validation,” Juan Carlos Guajardo, executive director of consultancy Plusmining, told MINING.COM. Beyond the reporting scandal, Fontaine delivered a stark assessment of Codelco’s financial performance, revealing that billions of dollars in investment have failed to reverse declining production while costs and debt have climbed. The company invested $32 billion over the past eight years, yet annual copper output fell from approximately 1.6 million tonnes to 1.2 million tonnes, Fontaine said. Codelco transferred $7 billion to the Chilean government over the past four years, 43% less than in the preceding four-year period, despite a 30% increase in copper prices. The company also increased its debt by 50% to finance those contributions, he said. Operating cash outflows rose 42%, while Codelco’s total cost per pound of copper in 2025 was 78% higher than that of a comparison group comprising three major multinational miners and Chile’s three largest mining operations. Fontaine also criticized the performance of Codelco’s major development projects, saying they had failed to deliver the production and financial returns originally expected from the capital invested. The figures highlight the challenge facing management as it attempts to restore profitability while maintaining the investments needed to sustain production. Fontaine said the board and new management are developing a recovery plan focused on improving profitability, generating cash flow and strengthening the company’s long-term financial position. The strategy will prioritize safety, profitability, operational and environmental sustainability, and stronger internal governance, including tighter controls, greater transparency and clearer accountability. Codelco also plans to pursue growth through public-private partnerships while directing capital towards projects capable of generating stronger returns. “For too long, the discussion has been overly focused on how many tons Codelco produced, and that hasn’t been immune to generating false production figures. But we have to ask ourselves how much value each ton generates and how much return each dollar invested delivers,” Fontaine said. The shift comes as Codelco expects copper production in 2026 to be closer to 1.2 million tonnes, with annual output projected at around 1.3 million tonnes over the following four years. Fontaine acknowledged that restoring confidence would require stronger inventory audits, more effective oversight and greater individual accountability for operational decisions. “There will be difficult times and the process will take time,” he said. title: World Bank sees gold holding above $4,000 through 2028, but warns silver faces steeper correction - Kitco
body: (Kitco News) - Gold and silver prices are expected to remain historically elevated through 2027, but investors should not expect a repeat of the explosive gains and volatility that defined 2026, according to the latest report from the World Bank. In its October Commodity Markets Outlook, analysts at the World Bank forecast gold prices to average $4,600 an ounce this year, a 33.6% increase from 2025. However, the bank expects prices to fall 7.6% to an average of $4,250 an ounce in 2027, followed by a further 5.9% decline to $4,000 in 2028. The outlook is slightly more bearish than the bank's April forecast, which projected gold prices averaging $4,700 this year and $4,300 in 2027. Silver is expected to face even greater downside pressure after significantly outperforming gold this year. The World Bank forecasts silver prices to average $70 an ounce in 2026, representing a nearly 76% annual gain. Prices are then expected to fall more than 11% to $62 an ounce in 2027 and another 6.5% to $58 in 2028. Although the analysts expect both precious metals to lose some momentum, their forecasts suggest that prices will remain well above historical averages as geopolitical uncertainty and demand for portfolio diversification continue to provide long-term support. The World Bank expects its broader precious metals price index to rise nearly 40% this year before declining 8.3% in 2027 and another 6% in 2028. Despite the projected correction, prices are expected to remain more than three times their average levels between 2015 and 2019. The relatively cautious outlook comes as the gold market struggles to regain its footing following a historic rally that pushed prices to record highs earlier this year. World Bank noted that gold prices fell 5% in the third quarter, with selling pressure continuing into October. The bank noted that rising government bond yields, expectations of tighter monetary policy and a stronger U.S. dollar have weighed on investor sentiment. The Federal Reserve's September interest rate increase, along with similar moves by other major central banks, has created significant headwinds for non-yielding assets such as gold and silver. At the same time, a dramatic shift in bullish speculative positions has added to recent selling pressure. However, the World Bank noted that gold's underlying fundamentals remain relatively healthy, particularly as investors and central banks continue to diversify their financial holdings. According to the report, investment demand and central bank purchases accounted for roughly half of global gold demand during the first six months of 2026. Although both sources of demand are expected to moderate over the next two years, they should continue to provide a solid foundation for prices. The bank also noted that central bank gold purchases have started to increase again after slowing earlier in the year, suggesting that official-sector demand could provide additional upside support. However, not all segments of the gold market are expected to remain resilient. Jewelry demand has declined sharply since 2023, and the World Bank expects consumption to remain weak as elevated prices discourage buyers. On the supply side, mine production is expected to increase only modestly, while higher prices should continue to encourage recycling. title: Lundin cuts copper outlook again as Chile weather bites - The Northern Miner
body: Lundin Mining (TSX: LUN) has lowered its annual copper production forecast for the second time since August as snowmelt continues to disrupt its Caserones mine in Chile, despite stronger-than-expected quarterly cash flow. The miner cut Caserones’ target to 105,000–115,000 tonnes from 120,000–130,000 tonnes, reducing company-wide guidance to 285,000–310,000 tonnes from 300,000–325,000 tonnes. The mine began the year targeting 130,000–140,000 tonnes before an August reduction . “Importantly, these are deferred tonnes rather than lost production, and we expect to see a recovery in operational performance through 2027,” president and CEO Jack Lundin said in the company’s quarterly results , released Wednesday. Reaching the midpoint of the reduced forecast requires about 78,000 tonnes in the fourth quarter, a 25% increase from the third, BMO Capital Markets analyst Matthew Murphy said Thursday. That puts pressure on Caserones to recover while Candelaria maintains strong grades and Chapada delivers steady output, as Lundin approaches a major investment decision at Vicuña. Lundin shares traded 10% weaker at C$28.48 Thursday morning in Toronto, giving the company a market value of about C$24.3 billion. Power outages caused by severe winter storms halted Caserones for about 30 days during the third quarter, including time needed to thaw flotation equipment and restart mills. Subsequent snowmelt has reduced haulage rates and restricted ore deliveries into the fourth quarter. The mine is about 125 km southeast of Copiapó in Chile’s Atacama region. Company-wide copper production reached 62,610 tonnes in the three months to Sept. 30, matching BMO’s forecast but missing the 68,000-tonne consensus estimate, Murphy said. Gold output of 36,763 oz. exceeded his estimate and roughly matched consensus. Caserones’ annual cash cost guidance remains $2.15–$2.35 per lb., following an increase in August. Consolidated guidance remains $1.95–$2.15 per lb. Candelaria’s copper production rose 13% from the second quarter, while Chapada in Brazil recorded its highest quarterly copper and gold output of the year. Free cash flow reached $312 million (C$436 million), exceeding BMO’s $14-million forecast and consensus of $219 million. Capital spending was lower than expected, while a $61-million working-capital release boosted operating cash flow, Murphy said. Desjardins analyst Bryce Adams described the results as mixed, with lower operating costs and stronger realized copper prices helping offset weaker sales volumes. Adjusted earnings of 32¢ a share exceeded his 28¢ forecast, but the reduced annual copper production range fell below his estimate of 314,000 tonnes. He maintained a buy rating and C$45 target. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $648 million also exceeded forecasts. However, that measure excluded $58 million in Caserones fixed overhead costs that BMO had included in its estimate, he said. Lundin ended September with net cash of $237 million. It also lowered annual capital spending guidance by $50 million to $980 million, including a $20-million reduction in sustaining spending at Caserones. Lundin is targeting a year-end investment decision at Vicuña , its equal partnership with BHP (ASX, LSE, NYSE: BHP). The project combines the Josemaría and Filo del Sol copper-gold deposits along the Argentina-Chile border. The venture has secured a provincial agreement with San Juan and approval for a high-voltage powerline connecting the project to Argentina’s grid. Engineering, financing arrangements and an updated first-stage capital estimate remain part of the work towards sanctioning. At Chapada, construction of an additional ball mill is about 15% complete, with commissioning targeted for late 2027. The Vicuña investment decision, project optimization and capital-cost update are the key upcoming events for Lundin’s shares, Murphy said. BMO maintained an outperform rating and C$49 target.

title: Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: LONDON -- Bank of England raises main interest rate a quarter point to 4% as Iran war stokes inflation. THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below. The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates Thursday for the first time in more than three years in order to tackle the inflation shock caused by the Iran war . With inflation predicted to rise further over the coming months, economists reckon the nine policymakers on the Monetary Policy Committee have little option but to increase the bank's key rate to 4% from 3.75%. The anticipated increase would be the first since August 2023. The pressure on rate-setters has grown steadily over recent months, but the rise in inflation to an 11-month high of 3.5% in September — above their target of 2% — cemented market expectations of a rate hike this month and potentially more in 2027. The main cause behind the spike in inflation this year has been the sharp rise in fuel costs as a result of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. “We imagine that many committee members’ patience with the recent rise in inflation has worn thin," said Ellie Henderson, an economist at Investec. “The longer energy prices remain elevated, the greater the risk that a temporary price shock becomes more permanent." Accompanying the expected rate hike will be the bank’s quarterly economic projections, notably those for inflation and growth. Higher interest rates cool the economy by making it more expensive to borrow, thereby bearing down on spending and inflation, but growth too. Those projections are highly uncertain though — even more so than usual — because the economic outlook hinges hugely on what happens with regard to the Iran war. The heavy losses suffered by the Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections have resulted in a sharp fall in energy prices . If the falls in oil and gas prices are sustained over the coming weeks, then the upcoming peak in inflation will likely be lower, which could temper expectations of further rate hikes, not just by the Bank of England. Others, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently in response to the higher inflation stoked by the Iran war, and forecasts for their interest rate strategy are largely contingent on what happens to the price of energy. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

title: Bank of Canada keeps 2% inflation target in mandate renewal - BNN Bloomberg
body: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada and federal government have agreed to keep a target of two per cent inflation at the core of the central bank’s mandate. The Bank of Canada sets its benchmark interest rate independently from the federal government but it gets its inflation-targetting mandate from Ottawa. The Bank of Canada said in a release announcing the renewal of its five-year mandate today that its inflation target has served Canadians well in recent decades. The central bank will continue to set monetary policy to make sure annual inflation dips neither too far below or above two per cent, but it retains flexibility to respond to economic shocks. The Bank of Canada increased its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years last week as monetary policymakers fear inflationary pressures could start to spread. The bank announced the mandate renewal minutes after the federal Liberals outlined its economic projections and fiscal track in Budget 2026 on Thursday.
